title: Senior's toolkit: Dictionary, HashSet and friends
summary: The hashing APIs .NET engineers use daily: single-lookup counting, comparers, frozen lookups, and keys that do not get lost.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: Dictionary, HashSet and friends
steps.body: Hash maps and sets are the most used data structures in real code. The difference between junior and senior use is in the details: one lookup instead of two, the right comparer, and keys that keep their hash.

toolkit.what: Look up a key that might be missing, in one lookup. The indexer `dict[key]` throws `KeyNotFoundException` for a missing key.
flags: a value or a default in one call
add only if absent; false otherwise (the indexer would overwrite)
toolkit.example:
if (!rates.TryGetValue(currency, out var rate))
    return Results.BadRequest($"Unknown currency {currency}");

toolkit.what: Get a reference to the value slot, adding a default if the key is new: counting with one hash lookup instead of two (`System.Runtime.InteropServices`).
flags: tells you whether the key was already there
update the stored value in place
toolkit.example:
foreach (var word in words)
    CollectionsMarshal.GetValueRefOrAddDefault(counts, word, out _)++;

toolkit.what: Every hash collection takes a comparer. Choose it on purpose: emails, tags and file names usually need case-insensitive keys.
flags: exact bytes; the fastest, the default for string keys
returns false if it was already there: check and insert in one call

toolkit.what: LINQ counting and aggregating per key without building groups (.NET 9+). Clearer than `GroupBy(...).Select(g => g.Count())` and cheaper.
flags: turn the pairs into a dictionary

toolkit.what: Read-only collections optimised for lookups (`System.Collections.Frozen`, .NET 8+). Slower to build, faster to read: ideal for config, lookup tables and allow-lists built once at startup.
A custom key type needs `Equals` and `GetHashCode` that agree. A `record` or `record struct` writes both for you. Never change a field a key's hash depends on while it is in a dictionary.
flags: record struct Point(int X, int Y)
value equality and hashing for free
when you write GetHashCode by hand
pass custom equality to the dictionary instead
toolkit.example:
readonly record struct GridCell(int Row, int Col);
var visited = new HashSet<GridCell>();

code: foreach (var w in "Apple apple APPLE pear".Split(' '))
steps.explain: With `OrdinalIgnoreCase`, all three spellings of apple are one key. Without the comparer it would print `4 1`.

steps.prompt: The currency converter fails for some users with this exception. What is the senior fix?
code: System.Collections.Generic.KeyNotFoundException: The given key 'gbp' was not present in the dictionary.
at Rates.Convert(Decimal amount, String currency) in Rates.cs:line 18
options: Build the dictionary with `StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase`, and use `TryGetValue` to answer "unknown currency" instead of crashing
Add `"gbp"` as a second key next to `"GBP"`
steps.explain: Two problems: the key's case and the missing-key handling. `ContainsKey` followed by the indexer does two lookups where `TryGetValue` does one, and duplicating keys for each spelling does not scale.

steps.prompt: Match each API to its job.
pairs: insert only if the key is new
insert, and learn whether it was a duplicate
count items per key without groups
an allow-list built once at startup
read with a fallback for a missing key

steps.prompt: Orders are kept in `Dictionary<OrderKey, Order>`, where `OrderKey` is a class whose `GetHashCode` uses its `Code` property. After code runs `key.Code = key.Code.Trim();`, `dict.ContainsKey(key)` returns false, yet the entry is still in `dict.Values`. Why?
options: The entry sits in the bucket for the old hash. Changing a field the hash uses strands it. Make key types immutable (a `record struct` with init-only fields)
Dictionary keys are copied, so the change did not reach the dictionary
`Trim` creates a new string, which breaks reference equality
steps.explain: A hash map finds a key by its hash at lookup time. Mutate the key and the lookup goes to a different bucket. Immutable keys make this bug impossible.

steps.prompt: Count words with a single hash lookup per word.
steps.explain: `GetValueRefOrAddDefault` returns a `ref int` to the slot, adding `0` for a new word, so `++` updates the stored count. `GetValueRefOrNullRef` does not add missing keys.

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: Every time you create a dictionary or set of strings, decide the comparer. Use `TryGetValue` wherever a key can be missing, records for composite keys, and frozen collections for lookup tables that never change after startup.
